title: What gospel did Jesus preach?
question: When Jesus went around 'preaching the gospel', what exactly was the good news he announced, and how do scholars disagree about it?
plainAnswer: Jesus' good news was that God was at last becoming king, as Israel's prophets had promised, and that this reign was breaking in through him. He called people to turn around (repent), trust this news, and follow him. He showed what the kingdom looked like by healing the sick, freeing the oppressed, eating with outsiders and forgiving sinners, and he explained it in parables. As his ministry went on he said plainly that he must suffer, die and rise, and he gave that death a saving meaning at the Last Supper. Scholars agree that 'the kingdom of God' was the centre of his message; they disagree about whether he thought of it as mostly present, mostly future, or both at once.
keyTakeaways: Jesus' headline was 'the kingdom of God has come near' (Mark 1:15), not a general invitation to go to heaven when you die.
'Kingdom of God' means God's active rule or reign more than a place; it draws on Isaiah's herald of good news and Daniel's vision of the Son of Man.
Healings, exorcisms and table fellowship with sinners were presented as signs that the reign of God was already arriving.
Jesus did warn of judgment, including Gehenna, and did promise life in the age to come; these sit inside the kingdom message rather than replacing it.
He predicted his death and resurrection and interpreted his death as a ransom and covenant sacrifice, which links his preaching to the apostles' later preaching about him.
The main scholarly debate is timing: future and imminent (Weiss, Schweitzer), already fully present (Dodd), or already and not yet (Ladd, Meier, Dunn, Wright and most today).

sections.heading: The headline: God's kingdom has come near
sections.body:
Mark sums up Jesus' preaching in one sentence: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom of God has come near, repent and believe the good news (Mark 1:14-15). Matthew describes him going through Galilee 'preaching the gospel of the kingdom' and healing every disease (Matt 4:23; Matt 9:35). Luke has Jesus say that he must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to other towns too, 'for this is why I was sent' (Luke 4:43).

The word 'gospel' (Greek *euangelion*) simply means good news, especially news of a victory or a new ruler. In the Roman world it was used of the birth and accession of emperors; a famous inscription from Priene in Asia Minor (9 BC) calls Augustus' birthday the beginning of good news for the world. Jesus' hearers, though, would have heard the word mainly through Isaiah, where a messenger runs to Jerusalem with news that 'your God reigns' (Isa 52:7; Isa 40:9).

So the gospel Jesus preached was first of all an announcement about God, not a technique for individuals. The fitting response was to repent (change direction) and believe (trust and commit to) the news.

callout.text: Myth: 'the gospel of the kingdom' and 'the gospel of grace' are two different gospels. Some dispensational writers have drawn this distinction, but most interpreters across traditions see one gospel: Jesus announced the kingdom, and the apostles announced the same kingdom now opened through his death and resurrection (Acts 8:12; Acts 28:31).

sections.heading: Old Testament roots: Isaiah's herald, Isaiah 61 and Daniel 7
sections.body:
Jesus did not invent the idea of God's kingdom. Israel already sang that the Lord is king, and the prophets looked forward to a day when God would act decisively to rescue his people, deal with evil and rule over all nations (Isa 52:7-10; Mic 4:1-4; Zech 14:9).

In Nazareth, Luke says, Jesus read Isaiah 61: the Spirit of the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind and freedom to the oppressed, and to proclaim the year of the Lord's favour. Then he said, 'Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:16-21; Isa 61:1-2). 'The year of the Lord's favour' echoes the Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and land returned (Lev 25:8-12).

Daniel 7 supplies the other key picture. After a series of beast-like empires, 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion, which is then shared with the holy people of the Most High (Dan 7:13-14; Dan 7:27). Jesus' favourite self-description, 'the Son of Man', and his answer at his trial (Mark 14:61-62) tie his mission to this vision of God's kingdom replacing the empires.

callout.text: Luke quotes Isaiah 61:1-2 but stops before 'and the day of vengeance of our God'. Many readers see this as deliberate: the present phase of Jesus' ministry is favour and release, with judgment still to come. Others think too much is made of where a reading ended.

sections.heading: What 'the kingdom of God' meant
sections.body:
In the Gospels 'kingdom' (Greek *basileia*) usually means God's reign, his rule in action, rather than a territory or a place in the sky. Matthew mostly says 'kingdom of heaven', following the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding the word God; it means the same thing as 'kingdom of God' in Mark and Luke (compare Matt 19:23-24).

The kingdom is something people can enter, receive like children, seek first, inherit and pray for (Mark 10:15; Matt 6:33; Matt 25:34). The Lord's Prayer defines it by parallel: your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as in heaven (Matt 6:10). So the hope is that heaven's rule comes to earth, not that people leave earth for heaven.

At the same time it has an end-time side. Many will come from east and west to feast with Abraham in the kingdom (Matt 8:11-12), the Twelve will judge Israel's tribes in the renewal of all things (Matt 19:28), and Jesus will not drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom (Mark 14:25).

sources.author: John P. Meier
sources.title: A Marginal Jew, vol. 2: Mentor, Message, and Miracles

sections.heading: Parables: the kingdom told in stories
sections.body:
Jesus explained the kingdom mainly through parables, short stories drawn from farming, households, money and feasts. Several make the same surprising point: the kingdom starts small and hidden but grows to fill everything, like a mustard seed or yeast in dough (Mark 4:30-32; Matt 13:33), or seed that grows while the farmer sleeps (Mark 4:26-29).

Other parables stress its worth and the response it demands: the hidden treasure and the pearl worth selling everything for (Matt 13:44-46). Some warn that the good and bad will be sorted only at the end (Matt 13:24-30; Matt 13:47-50). The great banquet shows the poor, the crippled and outsiders filling the places that invited guests refused (Luke 14:15-24). The lost sheep, coin and son show God's joy over one sinner who repents (Luke 15).

Jesus also said parables both reveal and conceal: they open the kingdom to those willing to hear and leave the hard-hearted puzzled (Mark 4:10-12). They invite the hearer to make a judgment and so to take a side.

sections.heading: Healings, exorcisms and meals as signs
sections.body:
When John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus pointed to what was happening: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news preached to them (Matt 11:2-6). These phrases echo Isaiah's pictures of God's coming rescue (Isa 35:5-6; Isa 61:1).

He treated exorcisms the same way: if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Luke 11:20; Matt 12:28). The strong man is being tied up and his house plundered (Mark 3:27). When he sent out the Twelve and the seventy-two, their instructions were to heal and to say that the kingdom had come near (Matt 10:7-8; Luke 10:9).

His meals mattered too. Eating with tax collectors and sinners was a public sign that God was welcoming the lost back (Mark 2:15-17; Luke 15:1-2). Almost all historians, including sceptical ones, accept that Jesus was known as a healer and exorcist; they differ about how to explain the reports.

sections.heading: Forgiveness, repentance and the call to follow
sections.body:
Jesus announced forgiveness directly, which shocked his critics: 'Son, your sins are forgiven', followed by healing as proof that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive (Mark 2:1-12). He told a sinful woman that her faith had saved her (Luke 7:36-50) and declared that salvation had come to Zacchaeus' house (Luke 19:1-10).

The welcome came with a demand. Repent, he said, or you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:3-5). He called disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross and follow him (Mark 8:34-38), and told a rich man to sell everything and follow (Mark 10:17-31). The Sermon on the Mount describes the kind of life the kingdom produces: blessing on the poor, the mourning and the persecuted, love of enemies, secret piety and trust in the Father (Matt 5:3-12; Matt 5:43-48; Matt 6:25-34).

In plain terms, grace and demand were not opposites in his preaching. The undeserved welcome was the reason for the costly change.

sections.heading: Judgment, Gehenna and the life of the age to come
sections.body:
It would be wrong to say Jesus never spoke about what happens after death. He warned of Gehenna, usually translated hell, more than anyone else in the New Testament (Matt 5:22; Matt 10:28; Mark 9:43-48). He spoke of a final separation of sheep and goats (Matt 25:31-46) and of the rich man in Hades (Luke 16:19-31). He promised 'eternal life', which in the Synoptic Gospels means the life of the age to come, the same as entering the kingdom (Mark 10:17; Mark 10:23-30).

But these warnings sit inside the kingdom message. Judgment is the other side of God putting the world right. Jesus' sharpest warnings were often aimed at the religious and the comfortable, not at outsiders (Matt 23:33; Luke 6:24-26).

How to read Gehenna (eternal conscious punishment, final destruction, or a purifying judgment) is a separate debate covered elsewhere in the app.

callout.text: Two opposite myths: that Jesus never mentioned hell (he did, often), and that his gospel was basically about escaping hell (his headline was the arrival of God's reign, with judgment as part of it). Both oversimplify the texts.

sections.heading: The cross and resurrection in Jesus' own preaching
sections.body:
From Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi onward, Mark records three explicit predictions: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and after three days rise (Mark 8:31; Mark 9:31; Mark 10:33-34). He then gives the reason: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), language that echoes the suffering servant of Isaiah (Isa 53:10-12).

At the Last Supper he interpreted his coming death as covenant blood poured out for many, and Matthew adds 'for the forgiveness of sins' (Mark 14:22-25; Matt 26:28). After the resurrection Luke presents Jesus teaching that the scriptures foretold the Messiah's suffering and rising and that repentance for forgiveness should be preached to all nations in his name (Luke 24:46-47).

Historians debate how much of the predictions' precise wording comes from Jesus and how much was sharpened after Easter. Most agree that Jesus expected a violent death and gave it meaning in advance, especially at the Last Supper.

sections.heading: How scholars differ: present, future, or both?
sections.body:
Johannes Weiss (1892) and Albert Schweitzer (*The Quest of the Historical Jesus*, German original 1906) argued that Jesus expected the kingdom to arrive very soon as a dramatic, world-ending act of God, and that he died trying to force its coming. This is called 'consistent' or 'thoroughgoing' eschatology. Texts like Mark 9:1 and Mark 13:30 are their strongest evidence.

C. H. Dodd (*The Parables of the Kingdom*, 1935) swung the other way with 'realised eschatology': in Jesus' ministry the kingdom had fully arrived; Luke 11:20 and Luke 17:20-21 were key. George Eldon Ladd (*The Presence of the Future*, 1974) and many others argued for 'inaugurated eschatology': the kingdom is already present in Jesus but not yet complete. This already-and-not-yet view is now the majority position, held in various forms by Meier, Dunn and Wright, and Dodd himself later moved somewhat toward it.

E. P. Sanders (*Jesus and Judaism*, 1985) placed Jesus within 'restoration eschatology': he expected God to restore Israel (the Twelve symbolising the tribes, the temple action pointing to a new temple). N. T. Wright (*Jesus and the Victory of God*, 1996) argued that Jesus announced the end of Israel's long exile and God's return to Zion, embodied in his own journey to Jerusalem and death.

callout.text: Luke 17:21 can be translated 'the kingdom of God is within you' (KJV) or 'among you / in your midst' (most modern versions). The first suggests an inner spiritual reality; the second points to Jesus' own presence. Most scholars prefer 'among you', since Jesus is addressing Pharisees, but the inward reading has a long history.

timeline.title: Jesus begins preaching in Galilee
timeline.note: After John's arrest, Jesus announces that the kingdom has come near (Mark 1:14-15). Exact year debated (27-29).

timeline.note: Jesus teaches in parables and sends the Twelve to preach the kingdom and heal.

timeline.note: Argues the kingdom in Jesus' preaching was future and apocalyptic.

timeline.note: *The Parables of the Kingdom* argues the kingdom had arrived in Jesus.

views.name: Consistent (future) eschatology
views.summary: Weiss and Schweitzer: Jesus expected an imminent, dramatic end of the age; the kingdom was wholly future and he was mistaken about its timing. Few scholars hold it in this pure form today, but its stress on Jesus' urgency is widely accepted.

views.name: Realised eschatology
views.summary: Dodd: the kingdom fully arrived in Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection; future language is symbolic of its significance. Valued for highlighting present fulfilment, but criticised for flattening the future sayings.

views.name: Inaugurated (already and not yet)
views.summary: Ladd, Kümmel, Meier, Dunn and most current scholars: God's reign truly began in Jesus but awaits completion at his return. Critics say it can become a way to avoid hard texts about imminence.

views.name: Restoration of Israel
views.summary: Sanders and Wright: Jesus' message centred on God restoring Israel and returning as king, with the nations then blessed. Critics question whether 'continuing exile' was as widespread an idea as Wright claims.

views.name: Moral and spiritual kingdom
views.summary: Older liberal Protestants such as Albrecht Ritschl and Adolf von Harnack (*What Is Christianity?*, 1900) read the kingdom mainly as God's rule in the soul and the ethic of love. Weiss and Schweitzer's work was largely a reaction against this view.

furtherQuestions: If the kingdom 'came near' in Jesus, what would it look like for it to be present today?
Why did Jesus speak in parables rather than plain statements?
How does Jesus' gospel of the kingdom connect to Paul's gospel of justification?
Did Jesus expect the end of the world within a generation, and how should Mark 13:30 be read?
Why is John's Gospel so different, speaking of 'eternal life' where the others speak of 'kingdom'?

title: What gospel did the apostles preach?
question: What did Peter, Stephen and Paul actually say when they preached in Acts, and how does that compare with Paul's own summaries of the gospel?
plainAnswer: The apostles preached about Jesus himself: God's promises to Israel have been fulfilled in him; he was crucified, but God raised him from the dead and made him Lord and Messiah; he will come again as judge; so turn to God, be baptised in his name, and receive forgiveness and the Holy Spirit. The sermons in Acts say almost nothing about going to heaven when you die and very little about hell; their centre is the resurrection and the lordship of Jesus. Paul's letters add a strong explanation of how Christ's death deals with sin and how people are put right with God by faith. Today scholars and pastors argue over which of these is 'the gospel' proper: the announcement that Jesus is the risen King (stressed by McKnight, Wright and Bates) or the message of justification by faith (stressed by Reformed writers such as Gilbert and Piper). Many say both belong together.
keyTakeaways: Every major sermon in Acts centres on Jesus' resurrection and exaltation, usually backed by Old Testament texts.
The usual call is: repent, be baptised in Jesus' name, receive forgiveness and the Spirit.
Speeches to Jews start from Israel's story; speeches to pagans (Lystra, Athens) start from creation and the one God.
Future judgment appears (Acts 10, 17); heaven as a destination and hell as a place are almost absent from the sermons.
Paul's own summaries (1 Cor 15:1-8; Rom 1:1-4) match the Acts pattern: Messiah, death for sins, burial, resurrection, appearances, Davidic Son of God.
C. H. Dodd (1936) argued for a common apostolic 'kerygma' (proclamation); his outline is still widely used, though critics think it too tidy.
The 'King Jesus gospel' versus 'justification gospel' debate is mostly about emphasis and definition; both sides affirm the other's elements in some form.

sections.heading: Are the speeches in Acts reliable?
sections.body:
Acts was written by Luke, most likely between about AD 70 and 90 (some argue for the early 60s). Ancient historians routinely composed speeches that captured what a speaker said or would fittingly have said; the Greek historian Thucydides says openly that he did this (*History* 1.22). So scholars debate how close Luke's speeches are to the actual words of Peter or Paul.

One camp (for example Martin Dibelius and later Ernst Haenchen) treats the speeches mainly as Luke's own compositions expressing his theology. Another (for example F. F. Bruce and Craig Keener) thinks Luke used sources and memory and that the speeches preserve early and genuine themes, noting old-sounding titles such as 'your holy servant Jesus' (Acts 4:27) and the absence of later developed theology. Almost everyone agrees that the speeches are summaries: Peter's Pentecost sermon takes about three minutes to read aloud.

Whichever view you take, the speeches are our best window on how the earliest church remembered its preaching, and they can be checked against Paul's letters, which are earlier.

sources.author: Martin Dibelius
sources.title: Studies in the Acts of the Apostles

sources.author: F. F. Bruce
sources.title: The Speeches in the Acts of the Apostles

sections.heading: Peter in Jerusalem (Acts 2, 3 and 4)
sections.body:
At Pentecost (Acts 2:14-40) Peter explains the outpouring of the Spirit as Joel's promise of the last days (Joel 2:28-32). He then tells the story of Jesus: attested by miracles, handed over by God's plan, killed by you, raised by God because death could not hold him (Ps 16:8-11), and exalted to God's right hand (Ps 110:1). The conclusion: God has made this Jesus both Lord and Messiah. When the crowd asks what to do, Peter says: repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:36-38).

In Solomon's Portico (Acts 3:12-26) the same outline returns, with new titles: God's servant (Isa 52:13), the Holy and Righteous One, the Author of life, the prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15). Peter calls for repentance so that sins may be wiped out, times of refreshing may come, and God may send the Messiah, whom heaven must receive until the time of the restoration of all things (Acts 3:19-21). He ends with the promise to Abraham that all families of the earth will be blessed (Gen 12:3).

Before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:8-12) Peter is brief: the healed man stands here by the name of Jesus, whom you crucified and God raised; he is the rejected stone become the cornerstone (Ps 118:22), and there is salvation in no other name.

sections.heading: Stephen's speech (Acts 7)
sections.body:
Stephen's speech (Acts 7:2-53) is the longest in Acts and the least like a standard evangelistic sermon. It is a defence against the charge that he spoke against the temple and the law (Acts 6:13-14). He retells Israel's story from Abraham to Solomon, stressing that God met his people outside the land (Mesopotamia, Egypt, Sinai) and that Israel repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent, such as Joseph and Moses.

His climax: the Most High does not live in houses made by hands (Isa 66:1-2), and you, like your ancestors, resist the Holy Spirit; they killed the prophets who announced the Righteous One, and you have betrayed and murdered him. Dying, Stephen sees the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:55-56), a direct echo of Daniel 7 and Psalm 110.

There is no explicit call to be baptised, because the speech is cut off by his stoning. It shows that early preaching could be prophetic confrontation as much as invitation.

sections.heading: Peter to Cornelius (Acts 10)
sections.body:
Peter's sermon in the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius (Acts 10:34-43) is often called the closest thing in Acts to an outline of a written Gospel. It begins: God shows no partiality, and the message he sent to Israel was 'preaching peace by Jesus Christ: he is Lord of all'. It then traces Jesus' story from John's baptism through his anointing with the Spirit, his doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil, his death on a tree, his resurrection on the third day and his appearances to chosen witnesses who ate and drank with him.

The sermon ends with the future and the offer: he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead, and all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name (Acts 10:42-43). The Spirit falls before Peter finishes, and the Gentiles are baptised (Acts 10:44-48).

This is the first sermon to Gentiles in Acts, but it still assumes hearers who know about Israel's God and Jesus' ministry in Judea.

sources.author: C. H. Dodd
sources.title: The Apostolic Preaching and Its Developments

sections.heading: Paul in the synagogue (Acts 13) and to pagans (Acts 14 and 17)
sections.body:
At Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:16-41) Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to David, then announces that from David's descendants God has brought Israel a Saviour, Jesus. Jerusalem's rulers condemned him, but God raised him, fulfilling Psalm 2:7, Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10. Then comes a line that sounds like Paul's letters: through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, and by him everyone who believes is justified (set free) from everything the law of Moses could not justify them from (Acts 13:38-39). It ends with a warning from Habakkuk 1:5. When the synagogue later rejects the message, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, and those appointed to eternal life believe (Acts 13:46-48).

At Lystra (Acts 14:15-17), facing a crowd who think they are gods, Paul and Barnabas urge them to turn from worthless things to the living God who made heaven, earth and sea and who gave rain and harvests as a witness. Jesus is not even named in this short report. At Athens (Acts 17:22-31) Paul starts from an altar 'to an unknown god', speaks of the Creator who does not live in temples and is not far from anyone, quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28), and then says God now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed, and has given proof by raising him from the dead.

The point: the content was adapted to the audience. With Jews, Paul argued from scripture; with pagans, he began with creation and the folly of idols, and led to resurrection and judgment.

callout.text: Myth: Paul's Areopagus speech was a failure he later regretted, which is why he said he resolved to know nothing but Christ crucified in Corinth (1 Cor 2:2). Acts reports converts at Athens (Acts 17:34), and nothing in the text says Paul changed his method. The 'failure' reading is a popular inference, not a statement of the text; scholars are divided on it.

sections.heading: Paul's defence speeches (Acts 22 and 26)
sections.body:
Paul's last speeches in Acts are courtroom defences, and they tell his own conversion story. To the Jerusalem crowd (Acts 22:1-21) he stresses his strict Jewish training, his persecution of the Way, the light on the Damascus road, Ananias' instruction to be baptised and wash away his sins calling on Jesus' name (Acts 22:16), and his commission to the Gentiles, at which point the crowd erupts.

Before King Agrippa II (Acts 26:2-23) he presents the gospel as the hope of Israel's twelve tribes: the resurrection of the dead. His commission is to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, so that they receive forgiveness and a place among those sanctified by faith in Jesus (Acts 26:18). He sums up his preaching: that people should repent, turn to God and do deeds consistent with repentance (Acts 26:20), and that the Messiah would suffer, be the first to rise from the dead and proclaim light to Israel and the nations (Acts 26:23).

sections.heading: Paul's own summaries: 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 1
sections.body:
In 1 Corinthians 15:1-8, written around AD 54, Paul reminds the church of the gospel he passed on 'as of first importance', which he himself received: that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and finally Paul. Most scholars think this is a very early formula, received perhaps within a few years of the crucifixion (Paul visited Peter and James around AD 35, Gal 1:18-19).

Romans opens with a similar summary: the gospel of God, promised beforehand in the prophets, concerning his Son, descended from David according to the flesh and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom 1:1-4). Its aim is 'the obedience of faith' among all nations (Rom 1:5; Rom 16:26). A few verses later Paul says the gospel is God's power for salvation, because in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith (Rom 1:16-17). Compare 2 Tim 2:8: remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, according to my gospel.

Paul's letters then explain these events at length: how Christ's death deals with sin (Rom 3:21-26), how people are justified by faith and not by works of the law (Gal 2:16), and how believers are united with Christ by the Spirit (Rom 6:3-11; Rom 8:1-11).

sections.heading: C. H. Dodd's 'kerygma'
sections.body:
In *The Apostolic Preaching and Its Developments* (1936) the British scholar C. H. Dodd compared Peter's sermons in Acts with Paul's letters and argued that they share one basic proclamation, which he called the kerygma (Greek for 'announcement'). In paraphrase, his outline is: the age of fulfilment has dawned as the prophets foretold; it has come through the ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus, descended from David; by the resurrection Jesus is exalted at God's right hand as head of the new Israel; the Holy Spirit in the church is the sign of his present power and glory; the age will soon be consummated by Christ's return; and therefore an appeal is made for repentance, with the offer of forgiveness, the Spirit and salvation.

Dodd distinguished this kerygma from didache (teaching for believers about how to live). His outline has been hugely influential in preaching and textbooks. Critics have pointed out that the distinction between kerygma and teaching is too sharp (Paul's letters mix them freely), that Acts' speeches vary more than the outline suggests, and that Dodd's own 'realised eschatology' may have shaped his reading.

sources.author: C. H. Dodd
sources.title: The Apostolic Preaching and Its Developments

sources.author: James D. G. Dunn
sources.title: Unity and Diversity in the New Testament

sections.heading: Allegiance to King Jesus or justification by faith? A current debate
sections.body:
Scot McKnight (*The King Jesus Gospel*, 2011) argues that many evangelicals have equated 'the gospel' with the 'plan of salvation' (how an individual gets saved), whereas the apostles' gospel is the story of Jesus completing Israel's story, as in 1 Corinthians 15 and the Acts sermons. Salvation is the result of the gospel, not its definition. N. T. Wright makes a similar case (*What Saint Paul Really Said*, 1997; *How God Became King*, 2012): the gospel is the royal announcement that Jesus is Lord, and justification is God's declaration about who belongs to his people. Matthew W. Bates (*Salvation by Allegiance Alone*, 2017; *Gospel Allegiance*, 2019) argues that the Greek word *pistis*, usually translated 'faith', often carries the sense of faithfulness or allegiance, so saving faith means embodied loyalty to Jesus as King.

Reformed writers have pushed back. Greg Gilbert (*What Is the Gospel?*, 2010) summarises the gospel as God, man, Christ and response: a holy God, sinful humanity, Christ's substitutionary death and resurrection, and the call to repent and believe. John Piper (*God Is the Gospel*, 2005) argues the ultimate good of the gospel is God himself, reached through Christ's work of forgiveness and justification. Piper, Thomas Schreiner and others have criticised Bates for blurring the line between faith and works, warning that 'allegiance' can make our obedience part of the ground of justification; Bates replies that allegiance is the response to grace, not a way of earning it.

Much of the disagreement is about definition and order. McKnight and Bates affirm substitutionary atonement and forgiveness; Gilbert and Piper affirm Jesus' lordship and the resurrection. The live questions are what belongs in the word 'gospel' itself and how faith relates to obedience.

views.name: Resurrection-and-lordship kerygma
views.summary: Dodd and many New Testament scholars: the apostolic gospel announced that the age of fulfilment had come in Jesus' death, resurrection and exaltation, calling for repentance. Strength: closely fits Acts. Weakness: may underplay the developed atonement theology in Paul.

views.name: Justification by faith at the centre
views.summary: Reformation tradition and writers such as Gilbert, Piper and Schreiner: the gospel's heart is that sinners are forgiven and declared righteous through faith in Christ's substitutionary death. Strength: fits Romans and Galatians. Critics: may read Acts' sermons too narrowly through later debates.

views.name: King Jesus and allegiance
views.summary: McKnight, Wright and Bates: the gospel is the story of Jesus as Israel's Messiah and the world's Lord; salvation and justification flow from it, and faith includes loyalty. Strength: fits 1 Cor 15 and Rom 1. Critics: risks confusing faith with works or obscuring individual assurance.

views.name: Diversity view
views.summary: Dunn and others: there was a shared core (the risen Jesus) but real diversity of expression between Jerusalem, Paul, John and others; no single formula was 'the' gospel. Critics: may overstate differences that Paul himself denied (1 Cor 15:11).

furtherQuestions: Why does Acts say so little about the meaning of Jesus' death compared with Paul's letters?
Should modern evangelism start from creation (as at Athens) or from scripture (as in the synagogues)?
Is 'allegiance' a good translation of pistis, or does it risk turning faith into works?
How should we understand 'the restoration of all things' in Acts 3:21?
If the apostles rarely mention heaven or hell in their sermons, why are those so central in many modern gospel presentations?

title: What gospel did the Church Fathers preach?
question: From the Didache to Augustine (roughly AD 90-430), what did Christian leaders say the good news was, what stayed the same as the apostles, and what new emphases appeared?
plainAnswer: The early Christian writers kept the apostles' core: one God the Creator, Jesus truly born, crucified and raised, coming again to judge, and salvation offered through repentance, faith and baptism. What changed was the emphasis. Facing persecution, they prized martyrdom; facing a pagan and philosophical world, they presented Christ as the divine Logos (Word); facing heretics who despised the body, they stressed the real flesh of Christ and the resurrection of the body; and as churches grew, baptism, the Eucharist and discipline for sin after baptism took centre stage. By the fourth century the Greek East often described salvation as theosis, sharing in God's life, while Augustine in the Latin West stressed sin, grace and the two cities. Whether these shifts were faithful development, decline, or a mix is a judgement, and Christians of different traditions answer differently.
keyTakeaways: The basic storyline of the apostles' gospel (Creator, Christ's death and resurrection, judgment, repentance and baptism) stays constant across these writers.
New emphases: moral rigour and the 'two ways', baptism and Eucharist as means of salvation, martyrdom, Logos theology, recapitulation and theosis.
Faith and grace language did not disappear: 1 Clement, Polycarp and the Epistle to Diognetus speak of salvation by grace or faith, not our works.
Forgiveness of serious sin after baptism became a major pastoral problem, leading to public penance (Hermas, Tertullian, Cyprian).

The kingdom hope shifted from imminent return toward the church's life and, for many from Origen to Augustine, a more spiritual reading of the end; early millenarians like Justin and Irenaeus expected an earthly reign.
Whether these were decline, legitimate development or a mixture is contested: Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox tend to read the same evidence differently.

sections.heading: Why these writers matter, and a word of caution
sections.body:
The 'Apostolic Fathers' (late first to mid second century) are the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament. Later 'Fathers' such as Irenaeus, Origen, Athanasius and Augustine shaped the creeds and the reading of scripture for all later churches. They are the bridge between the apostles' preaching and later Christianity.

Two cautions. First, most of what survives is letters, apologies and treatises, not evangelistic sermons; we see how they taught believers and defended the faith more than how they invited outsiders. Second, every tradition claims these writers: Orthodox and Catholics see continuity with their own teaching; Protestants find both early witnesses to grace and the seeds of later problems. The fairest approach is to let each writer speak in his own setting.

sections.heading: The earliest voices: Didache, 1 Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp
sections.body:
The *Didache* (a church manual, probably late first century, Syria) opens with two ways, the way of life and the way of death (Didache 1-6), largely drawn from Jesus' teaching on love of God and neighbour. It then gives instructions on baptism (7), fasting and prayer (8), the Eucharist (9-10) and ends with a call to watchfulness for the Lord's coming (16). Its gospel is mostly a way of life for those entering the community.

*1 Clement* (Rome to Corinth, about AD 96) holds up Peter and Paul as noble martyrs (5), urges repentance (7-8), defends the resurrection (24-26) and says plainly that we are justified not by ourselves, our wisdom or works, but through faith, by which God has justified all from the beginning (32.4), then immediately urges good works (33).

Ignatius of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom in Rome (about 110), insists that Jesus truly was born, suffered and rose in the flesh, against those who said he only seemed human (Smyrnaeans 1-3). He calls the Eucharist the flesh of our Saviour (Smyrnaeans 7) and the bread 'the medicine of immortality' (Ephesians 20.2), and he longs to be ground like wheat by beasts to become Christ's pure bread (Romans 4). Unity with the bishop is a recurring theme.

Polycarp of Smyrna, in his letter to the Philippians (about 110-135), echoes Ephesians: you are saved by grace, not by works, by the will of God through Jesus Christ (Philippians 1.3), and joins this to the resurrection, judgment and a call to righteous living (2). His martyrdom (about 155) was recorded by his church.

callout.text: Myth: grace and faith vanished from Christian teaching right after the apostles. 1 Clement 32.4, Polycarp, Philippians 1.3 and the Epistle to Diognetus 9 all speak of salvation by God's grace or through faith rather than our works. The opposite myth, that the early church taught Reformation justification in full, is also wrong: these writers combine grace with a strong stress on repentance, baptism and obedience without the later Protestant distinctions.

sections.heading: Hermas and the problem of sin after baptism
sections.body:
The *Shepherd of Hermas* (Rome, probably compiled about 100-150) was so popular that some churches read it as scripture. Its central message is a call to repentance addressed to Christians who had sinned after baptism. Hermas is told that after the great calling of baptism there is one further repentance available, but not repeated ones (Mandate 4.3).

This shows a real pastoral tension. Texts like Hebrews 6:4-6 and Hebrews 10:26 seemed to rule out a second forgiveness for serious sin, yet baptised Christians did lapse into adultery, fraud or denying Christ under persecution. Over the next century churches developed public penance: confession, exclusion from the Eucharist for a time, and readmission by the bishop. Tertullian (*On Repentance* 7-12) and later Cyprian of Carthage (*On the Lapsed*, 251) are key witnesses.

Protestant historians often see here the beginning of a move from grace toward a system of satisfaction; Catholic and Orthodox historians see a responsible pastoral development of Jesus' gift of binding and loosing (Matt 16:19; John 20:23).

sections.heading: Justin Martyr and the Logos
sections.body:
Justin (about 100-165), a philosopher from Samaria who taught in Rome, wrote two *Apologies* to the emperors and a *Dialogue with Trypho* the Jew. He presented Christianity as the true philosophy. Building on John 1, he taught that the divine Logos (Word or Reason) had been partly sown in all people, so that those like Socrates who lived by reason had a share in him, but that the whole Logos became flesh in Jesus (1 Apology 46; 2 Apology 10; 2 Apology 13).

Justin also gives the earliest description of Christian worship outside the New Testament: baptism as washing and illumination (1 Apology 61), and the Sunday gathering with readings, sermon, prayers, and bread and wine received as the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus (1 Apology 65-67). In the *Dialogue* he argues from the Old Testament that Jesus is the Messiah, and says he and other fully orthodox Christians expect a resurrection and a thousand-year reign in a rebuilt Jerusalem, while admitting other true Christians do not (Dialogue 80-81).

Justin was beheaded in Rome about 165. His Logos approach opened a long tradition of engaging philosophy; critics then and now worry that it let Greek ideas reshape the gospel.

sections.heading: Irenaeus: recapitulation and the restored creation
sections.body:
Irenaeus (about 130-202), who as a youth heard Polycarp in Smyrna and later became bishop of Lyon in Gaul, wrote *Against Heresies* (about 180) against gnostic teachers who said the material world was made by a lesser god and that salvation meant escaping the body. He answered with the 'rule of faith' handed down in the churches: one God the Creator, one Christ Jesus incarnate for our salvation, and the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets (Against Heresies 1.10.1).

His central idea is recapitulation, taken from Ephesians 1:10 where God 'sums up' all things in Christ. Christ re-runs the human story that Adam spoiled: obedient where Adam disobeyed, passing through every stage of life, and defeating the enemy as a man (Against Heresies 3.18.1; 3.18.7; 3.21.10). Irenaeus famously says that the Word became what we are so that he might make us what he is (Against Heresies 5 preface), and that the glory of God is a human being fully alive (4.20.7).

His hope is earthy. The last chapters of *Against Heresies* (5.32-36) expect the righteous to inherit a renewed earth in the resurrection, with creation itself restored. For Irenaeus, the gospel is God healing and completing his good creation, not rescuing souls from it.

sections.heading: Tertullian and Origen: rule of faith, rigour and restoration
sections.body:
Tertullian of Carthage (about 155-220) was the first major theologian to write in Latin. Later tradition says he had legal training, which shows in his style, but his identification with a known jurist is doubted. He defended the rule of faith against heretics (*Prescription Against Heretics* 13) and coined terms such as *trinitas* and *persona* (*Against Praxeas* 2). He was a moral rigorist: he taught that sin after baptism required humbling public penance (*On Repentance* 9) and later joined the strict New Prophecy (Montanist) movement. He used the language of 'satisfaction' to God for sins, which later Latin theology developed. His remark that the blood of Christians is seed (*Apology* 50) is often quoted in shortened form.

Origen of Alexandria (about 185-254), a teacher, biblical scholar and prolific preacher who later worked in Caesarea, opened *On First Principles* by listing what the apostles plainly taught: one God, Christ born of the Father before all creation and truly incarnate, the Holy Spirit, free will, resurrection and judgment (preface 4-10). His gospel is a journey: the soul is educated and purified by the Logos and ascends toward God. He also speculated that in the end God would be 'all in all' and all rational beings might be restored (On First Principles 1.6), a teaching linked to 'restoration' (apokatastasis, the word used in Acts 3:21). Some of his views were condemned in the sixth century, though how far he held the condemned positions is debated.

callout.text: Myth: Tertullian said 'I believe because it is absurd.' The phrase is not in his writings. In *On the Flesh of Christ* 5 he argues that the death and resurrection of God's Son are credible precisely because no one would invent something so unlikely. The paraphrase that became famous distorts his point.

sections.heading: Athanasius and the Cappadocians: incarnation and theosis
sections.body:
Athanasius (about 296-373), bishop of Alexandria and five times exiled for opposing Arianism, wrote *On the Incarnation*. Humanity, made in God's image, was sliding back into corruption and death; only the Word who made us could remake us. By taking a body and offering it in death for all, he defeated death and restored the image (On the Incarnation 6-10). His summary became a watchword of Eastern theology: he became human that we might become divine (54.3). This is the root of theosis (deification): not that people become God by nature, but that by grace they share in God's life and immortality (2 Pet 1:4).

The Cappadocian Fathers, Basil of Caesarea (about 330-379), his brother Gregory of Nyssa (about 335-395) and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus (about 329-390), defended the full divinity of the Son and the Spirit at the council of Constantinople (381). Gregory of Nazianzus argued that what Christ did not assume (take on) he did not heal (*Letter* 101), so Christ must be fully human, mind included. Gregory of Nyssa's *Catechetical Oration* is effectively a handbook on how to explain the faith, including the image of Christ's humanity as bait that caught death and the devil (24), and he too hoped that evil would finally be emptied out. Basil preached against hoarding wealth and founded a large complex for the poor and sick at Caesarea, showing that the gospel was expected to produce mercy.

sources.title: The Doctrine of Deification in the Greek Patristic Tradition

sections.heading: Chrysostom and Augustine: the preacher and the theologian of grace
sections.body:
John Chrysostom (about 349-407), 'golden-mouthed', preached through whole books of the Bible in Antioch and then as archbishop of Constantinople, where his blunt preaching against luxury led to his exile and death. His constant themes are repentance, the love of God, care for the poor and serious discipleship for ordinary Christians, not only monks. In his homilies on Matthew he urges hearers not to honour Christ's body with silk in church while neglecting him naked and hungry outside (Homilies on Matthew 50). His Easter sermon, still read in Orthodox churches, proclaims Christ's victory over death; its attribution to him is traditional.

Augustine of Hippo (354-430), a teacher of rhetoric converted in Milan in 386 (Confessions 8.12) and bishop of Hippo in North Africa, shaped Western Christianity more than anyone after Paul. Against Pelagius he taught that humanity is bound by original sin and cannot turn to God without prior grace, which God gives freely (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, 412). In *The City of God* (413-426) he describes two cities formed by two loves, love of God and love of self (14.28), and reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church (20.7-9), moving the West away from an earthly millennium. He also defended eternal punishment at length (book 21).

With Augustine, the Western gospel focused more sharply on the individual's sin, grace and eternal destiny, while the Eastern tradition kept its accent on incarnation, healing and theosis. Both, however, saw themselves as faithful to the same creed.

sources.author: Augustine
sources.title: On the Spirit and the Letter

sections.heading: What stayed the same, what changed, and how to judge it
sections.body:
What stayed the same: the story of one Creator God; Jesus as the Messiah and Son, truly human, crucified, raised and coming again; forgiveness of sins; the gift of the Spirit; the call to repent and be baptised; resurrection of the body and final judgment; a life of love, sexual purity and care for the poor. The creeds (Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381) are largely an expansion of the earlier rule of faith.

What new emphases appeared: (1) sacraments, with baptism and Eucharist described in realistic, saving terms; (2) martyrdom, prized as the perfect imitation of Christ; (3) moral rigour and post-baptismal penance; (4) Logos theology, presenting Christ to philosophers; (5) recapitulation and theosis, explaining salvation as the healing and transfiguring of human nature; (6) the institutional church and bishops as guardians of the true gospel; (7) a gradual cooling of imminent end-time hope after Constantine, and Augustine's spiritual reading of the millennium.

How to judge this depends on where you stand. Many Protestants (for example Thomas F. Torrance in *The Doctrine of Grace in the Apostolic Fathers*, 1948) argue that grace was soon overshadowed by moralism. Catholic and Orthodox writers (following John Henry Newman's *Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine*, 1845) see a faithful unfolding of what was implicit in the apostles. Many historians take a mixed view: real gains in clarity and depth, and some real losses, especially of the kingdom's earthly and communal hope and the simplicity of grace.

callout.text: Was the gospel 'corrupted' after the apostles? 'Corruption' is itself a judgement. Historians agree that emphases shifted (sacraments, penance, philosophy, hierarchy). They disagree on whether these were decline (many Protestants and restorationists), legitimate development (Catholic and Orthodox), or a mix (many historians across traditions).

views.name: Faithful development
views.summary: Catholic and Orthodox (and many Anglican) readers, following Newman and the Orthodox stress on Holy Tradition: the Fathers drew out what the apostolic gospel contained, especially about the incarnation, sacraments and the church. Critics say this can make any later development look inevitable.

views.name: Early decline into moralism and sacramentalism
views.summary: Many Protestants (Torrance, and in sharper form Restorationist and some Baptist writers): grace was soon overshadowed by moral effort, penance and priestly sacraments. Critics say this reads the Fathers through sixteenth-century debates and ignores their grace language.

views.name: Hellenisation
views.summary: Adolf von Harnack and others: the simple gospel of Jesus was recast in Greek philosophical categories (Logos, substance, deification). Critics reply that the New Testament itself already used such language (John 1) and that the Fathers often resisted philosophy at key points.

views.name: Mixed picture
views.summary: Many church historians across traditions: real gains (creeds, defence of creation and incarnation, care for the poor) alongside real losses (an earthly kingdom hope, simplicity of grace, the role of laity). This view asks each writer to be judged on his own terms.

furtherQuestions: Why did baptism and the Eucharist become so central in early Christian descriptions of salvation?
Was Justin right to see seeds of the Logos in pagan philosophers?
How is Eastern theosis different from, and similar to, Western justification?
Why did belief in an earthly millennium fade in the West after Augustine?
Is it fair to judge second-century writers by sixteenth-century questions?
